facts.statement: The research was a prospective observational pilot study carried out at a hospital in Sweden from 2021 to 2024.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: The study analyzed blood samples from 21 patients with acute ischaemic stroke and 19 control participants.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: The study compared stroke patients receiving a clot-removal procedure under anesthesia or sedation against a control group undergoing non-brain surgery under general anesthesia.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: Levels of three brain injury markers were measured in blood before the procedure and again at 2 and 24 hours afterward.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: In the stroke patients, the level of the marker GFAP rose significantly from the start of the study to the 24-hour mark.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: GFAP levels were higher in the stroke patients than in the control group at every time point measured.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: The control group did not show a significant rise in GFAP levels over the 24-hour period.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: The other two markers, NfL and tau, increased significantly in both the stroke patients and the control group.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: Because GFAP did not rise in the control group, the authors suggest it may be less affected by anesthesia and surgery than the other markers.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: The results support the need for further evaluation of GFAP as a potential blood marker for acute brain injury in hospital settings.
facts.subject: humans
